findings.point: The value ladder is three rungs, and the board is rung two only because it is the PROOF of rung one. Rung 1: a manager who deploys a routed team instead of one model doing every job (cost lever and quality lever in one mechanism). Rung 2: you can watch it — every agent, its ticket, its tier, its spend, on one page. Rung 3: nothing you say is lost, and it compounds — a mid-run request becomes a ticket, and a retro rewrites the stack. Under all three: hooks that refuse.
findings.why: Ordered this way the board stops being a feature tour and becomes the receipt for the claim made ten seconds earlier. That simultaneously fixes 'too little board' and the sceptic's 'prove it'.
findings.evidence: README.md:30 'hands each piece to a **dedicated subagent with fresh context and a model tier matched to how hard that piece actually is** … That is a cost lever and a quality lever at the same time.'

findings.point: The board should be on screen through the whole hero, not in a board chapter. Every mechanism line gets a board panel: routing → Spend 'by agent type'; nothing-lost → a card materialising in BACKLOG; a genuine decision → the Waiting-on-you card; hooks → a red refusal plus its row in 'Errors logged'.

findings.point: Five hook candidates, ranked. (1) 'Your most expensive model just renamed a variable.' (2) 'Your agents have a Kanban board now — and they move the tickets themselves.' (3) 'You are using one chat for everything. That is the mistake.' (4) 'Principal-engineer rates. Junior work. Every single session.' (5) 'Four and a half million tokens. Here is exactly where they went.'

findings.point: Of the eight pillars, four are genuinely differentiating and four are table stakes. DIFFERENTIATING: the interactive board (no competitor has one), hooks that actually block (evidence ✅ vs advisory/prompt, secrets ✅ vs ❌❌❌⚠️), state that survives restart and compaction in a committed journal, and per-role tier routing resolved from repo config with floors. TABLE STAKES AS A CLAIM: fresh-context subagents, the manager metaphor, statefulness, and 'self-improving' — every orchestrator says all four.
findings.why: The four table-stakes pillars still belong in the videos, but as the SETUP, never as the payoff — and each must be paid off by a differentiating mechanism within seconds, or the video sounds like every other agent-framework launch. The self-improvement pillar is rescued specifically by deletion: a retro that removes its own rules is a claim nobody else makes.

findings.why: It maps onto a universal daily annoyance — the aside you shouted into a chat window that vanished — and it is the pillar that makes the board feel like a place your intent lands rather than a status page. It also sets up the retro payoff: the request that recurs becomes a skill.

recommendations: THE VISUAL SPINE — "emit and return", and the desk never leaves frame. One element carries every cut: a brass-railed conductor card (16:9: a card centre-left; 9:16: a 3px brass rail down the left edge of frame, present from frame one). It is the only element that ever addresses the viewer straight-on, centred, gold-edged. Agents are ALWAYS off-axis, smaller, steel-railed, in columns. That single asymmetry reads as hierarchy with no labels: the manager faces you, the team faces the work. Three phases, repeated at three scales through the slate. BRIEF: your words arrive from off-frame top and land on the desk. SPLAY: agent cards are born at the desk's exact rect (GSAP fromTo seeded from the desk's own geometry, so they visibly come OUT of it) and travel to their columns — unequal distances, unequal arrival times, unequal sizes; the scout leaves first and arrives nearest. Never a symmetrical radial fan, which reads as a diagram. WORK: each agent card is a three-line mono micro-terminal that scrolls a fixed, deterministic line list. FOLD-BACK: an agent never fades out — it collapses to a compact chip, travels back along the path it left on, and lands on the desk, and on landing the desk's ledger line increments (`+1 merged`, sage). Cheap agents complete and return two or three times inside the time the deep agent is still out. That overlap IS the delegation story.

MODEL ROUTING WITHOUT A TABLE — the file, then the lamps. Beat one: the real `tiers:` block from templates/config.yaml types on, four lines, each with its own inline comment (`cheap: haiku # scout, mechanical sweeps, ledger bookkeeping` … `top: fable # security review, arbitration, final acceptance`). As each line lands, a lamp lights on the right — one agent card per tier. Beat two: the YAML slides away and only the four lamps remain, and the work runs. LIGHT IS THE COST METER: cyan glow intensity = model strength, ON-time = usage, per the palette's own doctrine. The `cheap` lamp is dim and on almost constantly; `work` pulses steadily; `deep` lights three times; `top` lights TWICE, for about two seconds of a twelve-second run, and is dark the rest. Split-screen it against "one chat": the same twelve seconds with a single lamp at full brightness the whole time. The frame's total light is the bill, and the Tyran side is visibly darker. No legend, no bar chart, no dollar figure needed until the Spend tab. Beat three, the floor (16:9 only): a `--risk low` request tries to dim the `top` lamp; it drops 20% and snaps back to full with a hairline mono tag `floor: top` — the escalation the product refuses to allow. Also show fresh context physically: a spawned agent's scrollback panel is EMPTY, one line in it; the one-chat panel's scrollback is a dense grey stack that keeps growing and pushes the useful line off the top of its own box.

THE TICKET BEAT — the best moment in the slate; build it as one continuous shot, ~4.5s in 16:9 and ~2.4s compressed in 9:16, with no cut. STAGE 0, the board is ALREADY live — do not introduce the board with this beat; the lanes are established and ticking before the interruption arrives. STAGE 1, THE INTERRUPTION: the operator's words enter in the SANS face, gold, unaligned to the grid, floating over the lanes with a real drop shadow, typed on with a caret — `also — rate-limit the webhook before we ship`. It must look like it does not belong on the board. Board dims 12% underneath. STAGE 2, THE SEIZURE (this is the shot): the conductor's brass rail reaches — its gold travels along the board's top hairline and strikes the floating sentence. On contact the letterforms snap from sans to MONO, snap left-aligned to the grid, and a card border DRAWS itself around them: a stroked rect animating stroke-dashoffset clockwise from the top-left corner, 0.45s. Text reflows inside the new box. A ticket id types into the corner: `T-9`. Mechanical, not magical — a box being drawn around a sentence. Land the snap on the word "ticket" in the VO. STAGE 3, THE FALL: gravity applies; the card drops into BACKLOG with one bounce (back.out(1.7), 0.5s), the lane header count ticks `(1)` → `(2)`, the lane border warms to --brass-edge for 0.3s and returns to hairline, the dim lifts. STAGE 4, THE RECEIPT, half a second later: one muted mono line under the top hairline, `journal: ticket.declare T-9 · appended`, which fades on its own. That line is why it is un-loseable rather than merely acknowledged. Then it is picked up immediately: rail turns steel, an agent name types beneath, card slides one lane right. Throughout stages 1-4, at least two unrelated things keep moving elsewhere in the frame — an age counter flipping, another card's rail pulsing. In the long explainer, show the beat a SECOND time at 0.4 scale in a corner while the main action continues, unremarked: this is just what it does now.

THE LIVE BOARD TOUR — tab order is the board's own, because the board's tab order is already an escalation of the operator's questions. The tab bar is ON SCREEN for every board shot in the slate; it is the thing that says "one real page", and it carries the `(2)`. (1) OVERVIEW, 4-6s: enter already scrolled to the tiles; the four tiles count UP into place — `waiting on you 2 · agents running 5 · progress 47% · needs a human 4`. Then the agent strip arrives stalest-first, staggered 0.12s, and ONE chip flips its age colour mid-shot from brass to sage because it just signalled. That colour flip is the cheapest possible proof the page is live. (2) BOARD, the longest hold — 12-14s in 16:9, 7-9s in 9:16. 16:9 renders the true 4-column lane grid natively with real titles from the captures (`T-6 — a clickable sandbox published with the docs`, `T-5 — a reboot-surviving resume`); 9:16 renders three lanes at a time and PANS laterally across the ten. Three things happen at once: the new ticket lands (the beat above), an existing card moves in-review → done and the done count turns sage, and the blocked lane's clay rail pulses once. Then THE CLICK: a card takes aria-pressed styling (brass border, brass-low fill) and the detail panel GROWS from under the lanes with its rows revealing top-down — `LANE / INITIATIVE / AGENTS / WORKED BY / LAST EVENT`. (3) WAITING ON YOU, 5-7s: the `(2)` has been visible since shot one, so arriving here pays off a promise. Slow push onto ONE question card. Reveal order inside it is the argument: kind tag `DECISION · A DEFAULT IS RECORDED`, the question, `RECOMMENDATION`, `DEFAULT`, `BLOCKS 1 ticket(s): T-5`. Then the answer box: caret, a short typed answer, the Answer button flashes brass, the card collapses to one sage line, and the tab count goes `(2)` → `(1)`. The counter decrementing is the last thing the eye sees before the cut. (4) SPEND, 6-8s, native rebuild: tiles, then the composition bar draws left-to-right and STOPS with cache read at 91% filling almost the whole bar — hold two full seconds on that, it is the most surprising true number you have. Then the ranked charts wipe in, then the TOKENS|COST toggle visibly flips and every label re-renders from `1.6 M` to a dollar figure. A toggle that works on camera is proof of a live page. (5) SETTINGS, long explainer only, 4s, and only for the refusal: KERNEL rows rendered locked with no control, and one dropdown that demands a second deliberate `Yes — loosen it` press.

THE RETRO — the loop closing, shown as three fates in one frame. Return to the desk (spine callback). All the initiative's tickets are in `done`, a column of sage-railed cards; the desk pulls them in and they compress into one line: `initiative closed · 7 tickets · 4 agents`. The retro agent is the only card that spawns AFTER everything else has come home, and it reads rather than writes: a cyan scan-line sweeps top-to-bottom over a tall thin column of mono journal lines, 1.2s — light moving over text, pure CSS gradient plus GSAP. Then three candidate lines resolve at three different times: (a) one RISES AND HARDENS into the knowledge panel, gaining a mono id `K-12` and an `applies_to` glob — sans becomes mono, the same words-harden-into-objects transition as the ticket beat; (b) one is REJECTED — the anti-bloat filter is drawn as four small gates it must pass, `recurs? · cost measured? · already covered? · one sentence?`, and it fails on `already covered`, which lights clay for a beat, then the candidate greys and drops out of frame; (c) one EXISTING rule that has been sitting in the panel since the shot opened, carrying `helped 0 / 6`, gets a strike-through and slides out. End with the panel holding the SAME number of rows it started with. That arithmetic on screen is the anti-bloat claim, and showing the rejection and the retirement is what makes the promotion credible to this audience. Then the graduation ladder as motion, never as a diagram: one entry has a tally beside it incrementing `••` → `•••`, and on the third dot it JUMPS one shelf up into `.tyran/knowledge/`; on the fifth it jumps again into a `CLAUDE.md` fence with the `<!-- tyran:rules -->` comment markers visible. Three shelves, one card climbing, 3 and 5 as real thresholds. CLOSING GESTURE, on every cut in the slate: the desk's outline gains ONE new gold hairline segment. That is the callback motif given a mechanism — the lash-stroke is not decoration, it is the thing the retro added.

HOOKS AS PROTECTION — five parts, and never end on the block. (1) SHOW WHAT IS IN DANGER FIRST: a diff, three ordinary files, and a fourth line carrying `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIA••••••••••••` (elided on screen exactly as the gate elides it — a refusal must never republish the secret, and being true to that is also good taste). The command types itself: `git commit -m "wire up the uploader"`. It is an ordinary, well-intentioned command; the agent is not being naughty, and that is the point. (2) THE STOP IS PHYSICAL, NOT AN ERROR: the brass rail that has represented the conductor all film thickens across the command's path; the caret hits it and the whole command block recoils 6px left, power4.out, 0.12s, ONCE. No shake loop. The line holds. (3) COLOUR DISCIPLINE: one `REFUSED` tag in clay, on screen under a second; the refusal body in muted text quoting the gate's real wording; the frame settles into brass. Red is the verdict, gold is the guard, and gold is what the shot is left holding. (4) THE COUNTERFACTUAL, 0.6s: a ghosted, desaturated frame rises behind the stop showing the same commit landing on a public remote, with one mono line — `a key published is a key burned` — and the brass line pushes it back down. This is the single element that converts "blocked" into "saved". (5) END ON THE PASS: the line becomes `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=${env}`, the command re-runs, `EXIT=0` in sage. Run the evidence gate on the same rhythm so the rhythm itself becomes legible as "this is what a gate does": a report reading `tests are green, everything works` recoils; it comes back carrying `# pass 343 # fail 0` and goes through, 5s for both. In the 16:9 explainer only, add the honesty beat — one small muted line under the passed commit, `blocks silence, not forgery`. It costs 1.2s and it is exactly what buys credibility with developers who distrust marketing claims. Cut it from 9:16.

PACING — 9:16 (18-45s, thumb-scroll, no rewind). One idea per 2.5-3.5s; a hard ceiling of five ideas in 28s and seven in 45s. First legible thing on screen by 0.4s. The BOARD must be on screen by 3.0s at the very latest — in a short the board is the hook, not the reward, and words can arrive over it rather than before it. Exactly one focal element per shot, occupying at least 55% of frame width. Type floors at 1080 wide: 26px minimum for any mono a viewer must read, 30-34px for load-bearing values, 62px for burned-in captions, 74-90px for a headline. Captions 2-4 words per cue, no cue over 0.9s. Transitions 0.30-0.40s, and they must OVERLAP the voiceover — the next shot starts during the last syllable of the previous line, never after it; this is the structural fix for "the pauses are too long". Never hold a frame longer than 1.2s without something moving in it. Board surfaces are rebuilt natively, never scaled captures. End on the lockup with the board still ticking behind it at low opacity and one age counter incrementing during the hold — that satisfies the no-frozen-final-frame ban with a real product behaviour.

PACING — 16:9 (95s hero, 240s tutorial). Hero: one idea per 5-7s, with the board sequence given a single continuous run of at least 12s — in widescreen the eye is moved by the camera, not by cuts, and a board that survives twelve seconds without a cut is the strongest possible claim that it is a real page. Tutorial: one idea per 8-12s, since the viewer expects to follow along; every ~35-40s a 1.2s chapter title that is NOT a full stop — the board stays visible at 25% behind it so momentum survives the break. Keep speech density at 85-92% and gaps at 0.35-0.8s, but add the rule that closes the operator's complaint: EVERY declared gap must contain a visual event — a lane count incrementing, a bar finishing its draw, a chip changing colour, a receipt line fading. A gap is a place for motion, not a place for silence. Voice, splitting the difference between the two rejected passes: confident, warm, assured, forward-leaning, landing the last word of each sentence — a person who has used this and knows it works, reading out a measurement they are pleased with. Not dry, not sold. Last 4s: lockup, board alive behind it, one counter ticking.

THE EIGHT MOTION RULES, 1-4. (1) THE DESK NEVER LEAVES — one element, the conductor's brass-railed card or the left-edge brass rail, is present in every scene of every cut; everything that appears is emitted from it and everything that finishes returns to it. No scene opens on an empty frame. (2) NOTHING FULLY STOPS — in every frame at least one true-to-product number is moving: an age, a token tally, a lane count, a composition bar. Use ages by preference, because the board genuinely computes them in the viewer's browser, so a ticking counter is accurate rather than decorative. The frozen final frame is banned outright. (3) THE CAMERA ACTS, THE LAYOUT HOLDS — cuts inside a board sequence are forbidden. The frame moves; the board stays one continuous object underneath. Three camera moves only: a slow push (scale 1.02→1.06 over 4-6s, sine.inOut), a lateral pan across lanes, and a snap-to that re-centres on a selected card in 0.35s power3.inOut. A tab change is a panel sliding under a persistent tab bar, never a dissolve to a new page. (4) TWO MOTIONS IN FLIGHT — no element waits its turn. Minimum two independent motions at any moment, three during board sequences. Staggers are unequal by design (0.11 / 0.16 / 0.22), never uniform, because a uniform stagger reads as a template.

THE EIGHT MOTION RULES, 5-8. (5) LIGHT IS MONEY — cyan glow encodes cost and nothing else: intensity is model strength, on-time is usage. Gold never encodes cost; gold is the operator's attention and there is only ever one gold thing in frame. Red appears only as a verdict, never as a fill, and never for more than a second. (6) WORDS HARDEN INTO OBJECTS — human input enters in the sans face, unaligned, floating, shadowed; machine state is mono, grid-aligned, bordered, flat. Every transition between the two is a DRAWN border plus a face swap landing on a beat, never a crossfade. One rule that covers the ticket beat, the answer box, the knowledge entry and the CLAUDE.md rule, so those four moments rhyme. (7) ONE RECOIL, THEN RESOLVE — a refusal gets exactly one 0.12s hard recoil against a brass line, one sub-second red tag, and must end on the passing case with a sage `EXIT=0`. No shake loops, no error iconography, no shot that ends on the block. (8) EVERY NUMBER KEEPS ITS RECEIPT — every figure on screen comes from this repo (`4.5 M tokens`, `$16.97`, `47%`, `8/17 merged`, `91% cache read`, `# pass 343`, `1314 unit tests`, `53/53`, `2 waiting on you`), set in the board's own mono at the board's own tokens. A figure may carry a 1s muted provenance chip beneath it (`from cost.mjs`, `board.json`). No invented numbers and none rounded for looks — the brief's mood is a measurement being read out, and this is the rule that enforces it.

BUILD SPEC, so the direction survives contact with the renderer. Rebuild every readable board surface natively in HTML at the board's exact tokens — `--bg #141210`, `--bg-raised #1c1a16`, `--bg-sunken #100e0c`, `--hairline #332e27`, `--brass #a8863c`, `--brass-bright #cfae63`, `--brass-low #221c11`, `--brass-edge #5d4c22`, `--steel #7d9ea9`, `--steel-bright #9dbcc6`, `--clay #c07a70`, `--sage #88a06a` — with the board's own 1px hairlines and 0.4-0.6rem radii, so drawn pixels and captured pixels are the same object and a wide capture can cut to a native close-up without a seam. Keep the tab bar in every board shot. Use real lane names in the real order (`waiting-operator · paused-limit · blocked · changes-requested · in-review · in-progress · ready · backlog · parked · done`) and real card titles from the captures. Screenshots are retained only for 16:9 establishing wides and for out-of-focus texture behind a lockup — never where a number or a sentence has to be read. Determinism: no Date.now, no Math.random, fixed line lists for every terminal scroll, and a hard `tl.set(..., {autoAlpha: 0, immediateRender: false})` kill written out one per line at every clip boundary so a seek past a fade does not leave a stale layer. Everything above is CSS transforms, opacity, stroke-dashoffset, background-position and GSAP — no video, no canvas, no external assets beyond the existing PNGs.

WHAT TO CHANGE FIRST IN THE EXISTING SLATE, in order of payoff per hour. (1) Replace the static `ask-q-1x.png` shot with a native question card that gets answered on camera and drops the tab count 2 → 1 — it converts the deadest six seconds in the slate into the most human moment in it. (2) Add the tab bar to every native board rebuild and plant `Waiting on you (2)` in the first board shot of every cut. (3) Move the board earlier: in the 9:16 board cut, open ON the lanes and let the kicker type over them; the kicker currently costs 4.4s of board time. (4) Add stage 4 to the ticket beat — the `journal: ticket.declare T-9 · appended` receipt — which is one line of markup and is the whole "never forgotten" claim. (5) Give the 91% cache-read segment its own two-second hold instead of a shared stagger. (6) Build the routing beat from the real `tiers:` block plus four lamps, and delete any drawn table. (7) Add the overnight two-shot from assets already on disk: the clay PAUSED banner, then the same board resumed with the agent strip refreshing. (8) Re-record voice at the midpoint — confident and warm, forward through each line, landing final words — and re-pack timings so every gap contains a visual event.
doNot: No purple-blue AI gradients, no bokeh, no stock developers, no drop-shadow card clichés, no light theme anywhere, no web fonts — system stacks only.
Never scale a 2240px board capture into a 1080-wide frame where anything has to be read; rebuild it natively or do not show it.
Never end a hook or gate shot on the refusal. The last state of any protection beat is the passing case with a sage EXIT=0.
Never let red be a fill, a background, or last longer than about a second. Red is a verdict; gold is the guard. No third accent colour under any circumstances.
Never use cyan as an accent — no cyan buttons, links, borders or highlights. It is a light source, and in this slate it is the cost meter.
No cuts inside a board sequence, and no board that fades in. The board is either already there or the camera arrives on it.
No frozen final frame, no infinite loop, no unseeded randomness, no Date.now or Math.random in any composition.
No invented numbers, no rounded-for-looks figures, and no fabricated UI. Every value on screen exists in this repo or in the captures.
No symmetrical radial fan-out, no org-chart diagram, no boxes-and-arrows explainer of the agent team. The hierarchy is shown by scale, axis and light, never drawn.
No browser chrome around the board, and no cursor arrow graphics — interactions are shown by state changes (aria-pressed styling, a caret, a button flash), not by a drawn pointer.
No uniform staggers, no easing on a single default, no element left as the only thing moving in a frame.
No shake loops, error triangles, sirens, or any iconography that codes a hook as a system failure rather than as a boundary being held.
Do not introduce the board with the ticket beat — the board must already be live and ticking before your words interrupt it.
Do not show the retro as an addition only. A promotion without a visible rejection and a visible retirement reads as bloat, which is the opposite of the claim.

result.headline: Seven of the operator's eight pillars are real, named and mechanically enforced — the one exception is "see how much money you saved", which exists nowhere in the codebase — and the sharpest proof of the whole tier thesis is already sitting in a captured screenshot: on one board, scout cost $0.03 while implementer cost $6.72.

findings.point: Single point of contact is literally one command. `/tyran:setup` runs once per repo and installs a bare `/tyran` shortcut; after that the operator types `/tyran` and describes the work in prose. `/tyran:status`, `/tyran:doctor`, `/tyran:retro`, `/tyran:hello` are the only other entry points.
findings.why: The video can show the entire user-facing surface in four lines of terminal. 'One point of contact' is not a metaphor here — it is the install instruction.
findings.evidence: README.md:162-172 — "/tyran:setup  # once per repo: scans it, writes .tyran/, installs /tyran" / "/tyran  # then describe what you want done"

findings.point: The interview is a specified protocol, not a vibe. The conductor asks only when the answer materially changes the plan, does not follow from the repo, and is a matter of taste/product/risk; it batches at most 4 questions, each carrying its own recommendation; after the plan is accepted there are zero questions except at gates; and "Shall I continue?" is forbidden in writing.
findings.why: This is the 'seasoned manager' pillar made concrete and quotable. 'At most four questions, each with my recommendation, then I don't bother you again' describes a real rule.
findings.evidence: skills/run/SKILL.md:105-116 and :301 — "Batch questions — at most 4 at once, each with your recommendation" ... "**\"Shall I continue?\" is forbidden.**"

findings.point: The roster is exactly four agents, and two of the tool grants are the story. tyran:scout = read-only recon plus Bash (git log, ls, command -v). tyran:implementer = all tools, one story, its own branch/worktree. tyran:reviewer = every tool EXCEPT Edit/Write/NotebookEdit. tyran:retro = improves Tyran, never product code.

Tier aliases live in ONE file: cheap/work/deep/top.

findings.point: Security review and arbitration sit on a FLOOR no cost profile and no risk flag can cross, and the floor is applied last so it cannot be shifted out of. When a floor corrects a request the tool says so on stderr rather than quietly handing back something else. On capacity loss a tier falls DOWN the ladder, never up, and never lowers the reasoning effort.
findings.why: This is the answer to 'cheap models sounds like a downgrade'. The cheapness is bounded by a mechanism, and the mechanism announces itself. 'It falls down the ladder, never up' is a strong, filmable stderr line.
findings.evidence: docs/agents.md:126-130 — "**Security review and arbitration have a floor** ... The floor is applied last, after the shift, so it cannot be shifted out of."

findings.point: 'Never forgets a request' is the conductor's mid-run queue rule: an operator message is triaged at the next natural pause into a `ticket.created` journal event carrying id, title, deps and predicted files, and the operator gets a one-line confirmation — "queued as T-9". The id comes from `journal.mjs next-id`, never from memory.
findings.why: The script should use the literal confirmation phrase 'queued as T-9' — it is the product's own wording. Honest nuance: this is a conductor protocol written into the skill, not a hook, and it fires at the next pause rather than instantly.

findings.point: The board is FIVE tabs and TEN lanes, and the captures carry real filmable numbers: 3 initiatives, 8/17 tickets merged (47%), Waiting on you (2), Agents running 5, Needs a human 4, a red PAUSED — overnight-mode banner, agent chips reading '5 HOURS since last signal — likely dead', two logged errors. Lanes: waiting-operator, paused-limit, blocked, changes-requested, in-review, in-progress, ready, backlog, parked, done.

The scout did the reconnaissance for four tenths of one percent of the implementer's bill, on the same board, in the same run.

findings.point: The retro is not a suggestion — a `Stop` hook refuses your session once. When every ticket in an initiative is merged and no retrospective has been recorded since the last merge, retro-gate.mjs blocks the turn and prints why. Deciding NOT to run one is legitimate: record a `retro.entry` of kind `skipped` and it never asks again.
findings.why: Completely unused in any script, and the strongest framing of pillar 7: Tyran will not let you walk away from the work without learning from it, exactly once. The refusal text is quotable verbatim.
findings.evidence: hooks/hooks.json:57-67 registers retro-gate.mjs on `Stop`; site/src/components/landing/Gates.astro:70 — "tyran: initiative \"earnings-recap\" has all 7 of its tickets merged and no retrospective recorded since the last merge."

findings.point: Self-improvement has a numbered graduation pipeline: a mid-run `finding` → a MISTAKES.md entry with a signature → at 3 recurrences a `.tyran/knowledge/*.yaml` entry pasted into every matching handoff → at 5 a one-line rule Tyran writes into your CLAUDE.md between `<!-- tyran:rules start -->` markers, carrying the signature and the dated entries that earned it. Deletion is preferred to addition; at most 3 changes to the conductor skill per retro; 'a retro that changes nothing is a correct outcome'.
findings.why: 'Three strikes and it becomes knowledge, five and it becomes law' is a whole vertical short, and the fence-with-dated-evidence is a beautiful screen-drawable artifact. The anti-bloat ceiling makes it credible rather than creepy.
findings.evidence: docs/self-improvement.md:144-163 — the pipeline diagram, "3 to knowledge, 5 to law"; :183 shows a real fence line "(`worktree-missing-deps`, 5 occurrences — MISTAKES.md entries 2026-05-02, 2026-06-11, ...)"

findings.point: Nine hooks across five platform events, and SEVEN of them can refuse: secrets-gate (PreToolUse/Bash), write-guard, policy-gate, usage-gate (PreToolUse), retro-gate (Stop), evidence-gate (SubagentStop), pre-compact (PreCompact). Two are probes that cannot refuse: session-start and board-refresh. The runtime makes refusal the default — you cannot approve, and any throw becomes a refusal naming the error class.
findings.why: 'Nine hooks. Seven of them can say no.' is a whole title card. The gate-vs-probe split is enforced in code: runGate throws if you register it on an event that cannot refuse.
findings.evidence: hooks/hooks.json:1-103 (nine registrations across SessionStart, PreToolUse, Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompact); docs/hooks.md:72-86 — "you cannot approve ... you cannot crash into an approval"

findings.point: The secrets gate's invariant is coverage arithmetic, not an exit code: the gate determines the payload and the target itself, hands the bytes to gitleaks, and refuses unless the scanner reports reading exactly the number of bytes sent. It scans every object a commit would add (markdown included), every commit not on the remote being pushed to, files uploaded by gh release/gist, and the command line itself. It refuses WITHOUT scanning: --no-verify and any unambiguous abbreviation of it, -n on commit, a core.hooksPath override, --force on push, and kill -9 in every spelling.
findings.why: 'coverage verified' is the phrase to put on screen — it appears verbatim in the refusal. The --no-verif detail (an abbreviation that skipped a live pre-commit hook while an equality check saw nothing) is the specificity senior developers reward.
findings.evidence: docs/hooks.md:190-193 — "The gate determines the payload and the target itself and hands the bytes to the scanner ... coverage is verified by arithmetic rather than inferred from an exit code."; hooks/scripts/secrets-gate.mjs:1812-1815 — "tyran secrets-gate: refused. N secret-shaped finding(s) ... (X bytes, coverage verified)."

findings.point: The policy gate refused ME, live, during this research session. Running `wc -l hooks/scripts/secrets-gate.mjs` returned a full-paragraph refusal naming the protected glob, the allowed read-only programs, the residual floor, and its own declared limits.
findings.why: Real captured refusal text, produced today, against an agent that had no intention of writing anything. Every gate here states its own limits inside the refusal — rare, extremely credible, and directly serves the 'hooks guard behaviour' pillar.
findings.evidence: live tool output this session — "tyran policy-gate: refused. This command names a path this gate protects. - \"hooks/scripts/secrets-gate.mjs\" is under the protected path `hooks/**` ... Declared floor: this reads the COMMAND, never the effect of running it. 6 known ways past it are listed in docs/policy-gate.md."

findings.point: FOUR THINGS ARE WRONG OR OVERSTATED. (a) There is NO savings number — nothing in cost.mjs, board-html.mjs, docs/cost.md or the board computes what you saved; the only 'saved' string in the codebase is a Settings-tab toast. (b) vo.json's 'you answer from the board' requires `--serve --write`; the card itself prints 'Needs the board started with --write.' (c) The Spend capture is labelled 'rate card sample-rates (invented)' with models named sample-large/sample-small. (d) README says 'Four tabs' (there are five) and '1314 unit tests' (measured today: 1405 pass, 0 fail).
findings.why: (a) is the operator's own pillar-6 wording and would be the most falsifiable claim in the slate — a developer who installs it looking for the savings figure finds nothing. (c) would publish the word 'invented' in 4K.
findings.evidence: grep over scripts/cost.mjs, scripts/board-html.mjs, docs/cost.md, docs/board.md, README.md for saved|savings returns only scripts/board-html.mjs:1074 (a Settings toast); video/assets/capture/hi-spend-cost.png reads "rate card sample-rates (invented)"; README.md:208 "Four tabs", README.md:260 "1314 unit tests"

recommendations: Rebuild the Spend By-agent-type chart natively in 9:16 and animate the four bars in descending order — conductor $8.73, implementer $6.72, reviewer $1.48, then scout at $0.03, barely a pixel wide. Hold on the scout bar. That is the tier argument won without narration. Relabel the models to tier-role names so the word 'invented' never reaches a frame.

Replace any 'see how much you saved' line with what the product actually does: 'You see what it cost. Per model. Per agent. Per ticket. Including the conductor's own share — 55% of the tokens, on its own row, because a table that hid it would show you a fraction of the bill.' The honesty is more persuasive than an invented savings figure and is fully backed by docs/cost.md.

Give the retro pillar the Stop gate as its climax: the operator tries to end the session, the terminal refuses once, the refusal scrolls — 'all 7 of its tickets merged and no retrospective recorded since the last merge ... This is the only loop through which Tyran learns from an initiative instead of repeating it.' Then cut to the CLAUDE.md fence line with its five dated MISTAKES.md entries.

Run the graduation pipeline as its own vertical short: 'Once is a finding. Three times and it becomes knowledge, pasted into every handoff that touches those files. Five times and Tyran writes it into your CLAUDE.md as law — with the five dates that earned it.' The 3→5 ladder is already an ASCII diagram in docs/self-improvement.md.

For the hooks cut, open on the live policy-gate refusal captured in this session (an agent naming a protected path and being told no), then the evidence-gate refusal verbatim from Gates.astro, then the secrets-gate line ending '(N bytes, coverage verified)'. Three refusals, three different gates, forty seconds. Title card: 'Nine hooks. Seven of them can say no.'

Write the interview beat with the real rule: 'At most four questions. Each one carries his recommendation. After you accept the plan he does not ask again except at a genuine gate — "shall I continue?" is banned in his own instructions.' That last clause is a literal quote and lands harder than any paraphrase.

Shoot the ticket capture as a two-shot: the operator typing a throwaway aside mid-run, the terminal answering 'queued as T-9', then the card appearing in the backlog lane of the natively-rebuilt board. Use the product's own confirmation wording.

For the board's flashiest eight seconds, animate the Overview tiles filling with the captured values — Waiting on you 2 · Agents running 5 · Progress 47% (8 of 17 merged) · Needs a human 4 — under the red PAUSED — overnight-mode banner, with the agent strip aging beneath it and one chip turning clay-red at '5 HOURS since last signal — likely dead'.

Name the four tiers on screen as roles, never as models: cheap · work · deep · top. The repo's own doctrine is that model names live in exactly one file, and a video that hard-codes one ages the moment a model is deprecated.

Reframe 'agents retain memories' — the truth is better and it is the actual differentiator: agents are deliberately disposable and start with fresh context; the STATE is what persists, in an append-only journal committed to your repo. 'The agents forget. The system doesn't. That is why the second opinion is a real one — an agent that never saw the last six failed attempts cannot inherit them.'

In the onboarding video, state the two real prerequisites rather than gliding past them: restart Claude Code after install (hooks and agents are read at session start), and the secrets gate needs gitleaks on the machine — 'no gitleaks means no commit' is deliberate, and a viewer who hits it without warning blames the product.

Every board shot must be the natively rebuilt HTML at 9:16 using the board's own tokens (--brass #a8863c, --steel #7d9ea9, --sage #88a06a, --clay #c07a70, bg #1c1a16, hairline #332e27) so drawn pixels and captured pixels are the same colour. The 2240px screenshots are reference for content and wording only, never for scaling into a phone frame.
doNot: Do not say Tyran shows how much money you saved, and do not put a savings figure, a percentage saved, or a before/after cost comparison on screen. Nothing in the repo computes a counterfactual. Say what it cost — per model, per agent, per ticket.
Do not film the Spend capture close enough to read 'rate card sample-rates (invented)', 'sample-large' or 'sample-small'. Rebuild that panel with tier-role labels.
Do not claim the evidence gate proves the work happened. It blocks silence, not forgery — the repo says so in its own README. 'It raises the price of a lie' is the honest and stronger line.

Do not show answering a question from the board without the served --write board. The card itself prints 'Needs the board started with --write', and a viewer who opens board.html from disk finds the box disabled and Spend missing entirely.
Do not quote '1314 unit tests' or 'four tabs' from the README; both are stale. Measured today: 1405 tests pass, 0 fail, and the board has five tabs.

Do not imply overnight mode is on by default — the shipped config carries `limits: mode: 'off'` and it needs the operator-installed statusline helper for telemetry. Show it as something you switch on.
Do not name a model (haiku/sonnet/opus/fable) in narration or on screen. Roles and tiers only — the repo's own test suite fails on a model name outside `tiers:`.

Do not narrate the routing as 'cheap models do the cheap work' without the floor. Unqualified it reads as a downgrade; with it — security review and arbitration cannot be dropped below the top tier by any flag — it reads as engineering.
No long pauses between lines, no dramatic trailing-off, and no breathless hype. Confident and warm: someone reading out a measurement they trust.

No frozen final frame, no purple-blue AI gradients, no bokeh, no stock developers, no light theme, no browser chrome around the board. Gold #d4a017 is the only accent — cyan is a light source, red is refusal, green is a ledger plus.

result.headline: The manager metaphor holds almost everywhere in this product — scoping, delegating by difficulty, refusing in mechanism rather than in prose, running a retro — but it breaks at exactly one place the operator's brief leans on hardest: the board reports what you SPENT, never what you saved, and every script must trade that savings claim for the far stronger one it can actually show ("the first bill you can check, per model, per agent, per ticket").

findings.point: THE THROUGH-LINE, AT THREE LENGTHS. Paragraph: "You are running a whole engineering org out of one chat window, and you are the only employee. Every job — the grep, the rename, the security call — goes to the same expensive model, which re-reads the entire conversation before it does any of them and forgets all of it when the window closes. Tyran is the seasoned engineering manager for that org. You brief him once; he interviews you until the goal is unambiguous, sizes the work, and hands each piece to a dedicated agent with fresh context and a price that matches the difficulty. Scouts scout. The expensive tier is held back for the calls that cannot be un-made. Anything you say in passing becomes a ticket on a board you can watch, and when an agent hits a real decision it comes to you with a recommendation rather than a shrug. None of it is enforced by asking nicely: hooks refuse the report with no evidence and the commit carrying a secret. And when the work closes, the team runs a retro on itself and writes what it learned into your repo — so the next initiative starts from a team that has already worked here." | Sentence: "Tyran is a seasoned engineering manager for your AI team — you stay the stakeholder, he does the delegating, the board shows you everything, and the team gets better every time you use it." | Five words: "A manager, not a chat." (alternates: "Stop chatting. Start delegating." / "One manager. A whole team.")
findings.why: Every cut is then a subset of one paragraph rather than five writers' separate guesses; the five-word version is the end card, the sentence is the YouTube description and the site hero, the paragraph is the slate's claim boundary — nothing may be said in a video that is not in it.
findings.evidence: Operator: "I like the approach with presenting Tyran as working with a senior manager that you drop work on him, and he's coming to you, discussing things with you." · README.md:21

findings.point: EMOTIONAL ARC. 0s — recognition with a small sting: "that's me," delivered as a diagnosis, never a scolding; the viewer must feel seen, not caught. 10s — relief: the org chart lands and the guilt converts into "oh, there is a shape to this." 30s — appetite: the board is on screen and MOVING, and the feeling to engineer is "I want that window open on my second monitor tonight." End — calm and restored agency: "I keep the judgement, I lose the grind, and it gets better." Deliberately not urgency, not FOMO.
findings.why: It also resolves the two contradictory voice notes structurally instead of by knob-twiddling: the read warms and settles in REGISTER as it goes while the pace stays constant. Excitement at 0s is accusatory; excitement at the end is a pitch. Confidence throughout, calm at the landing.
findings.evidence: Operator: "the voices are not excited enough" then "the voice in those two videos has TOO MUCH ENERGY" · "There is too little board in the videos."

findings.point: THE MAP THAT IS TRUE (the spine — writers may use any of these without hedging). Interview before work = scoping with a stakeholder. Tier routing = you do not put your principal on the grep. Role floors, where security review and arbitration resolve to the top tier under every profile and every risk level = some calls are never delegated downward — the single strongest mapping in the set. Reviewer has no Edit/Write = the person who grades the work cannot rewrite it. Fresh context per subagent = a new hire briefed on the ticket, not on the last six weeks. Journal committed to the repo = the manager's written record instead of the manager's memory. An ask carrying a recommendation and a recorded default = a good manager brings you a recommendation, not a question — and the card itself says which kind it is, "decision · a default is recorded" or "blocking · no safe default". last_evidence sorting above last_signal = the loudest person in standup is not the one shipping. Graduation 3 → knowledge, 5 → law = say it once it is advice, say it five times it is policy. .tyran/STOP = the andon cord, pullable from a phone without killing the run. Overnight wind-down = a handover at end of shift with the work written down, not dropped mid-sentence.
findings.why: These eleven are load-bearing and defensible line by line, which means a writer can be vivid without a fact-check round. They also give the slate eleven distinct scenes rather than one idea restated.
findings.evidence: docs/agents.md:20 "A reviewer who can fix what they found ends up approving their own patch" · docs/board.md:123-124 · docs/self-improvement.md:144

findings.point: THE STRETCHES — SEVEN PLACES THE METAPHOR LIES, MARKED SO WRITERS AVOID THEM. (1) Tyran is not a person or a process standing beside you: the conductor IS your own session, and its row in the routing table is explicitly advisory because nothing can change a running session's model. Never cut to a character who decides something your session did not. (2) "Agents talk to each other" — they do not chat; they append events to one journal and receive knowledge briefs. Chat bubbles between agents invent an architecture and weaken the real claim, which is that the conversation survives a restart. (3) "Agents are fully stateful, they retain memories" — a subagent is deliberately STATELESS; that is the entire fresh-context argument. Truthful and stronger: the TEAM remembers, each agent starts clean. Getting this wrong contradicts your own best beat inside the same video. (4) "Never forgets" — minting the ask is mechanical, but deciding a passing remark deserves a ticket is model behaviour. Say "it goes on the board," not "it is impossible to lose." (5) "The retro notices you were annoyed" — the retro reads journals, ledgers, reports and git history, not your mood, and a retro that changes nothing is a correct outcome. (6) "Hooks prevent secrets from being committed" — the docs refuse that guarantee by measurement. (7) "The evidence gate makes reports honest" — it blocks silence, not forgery.
findings.why: Each of these is a claim a senior developer can disprove in ten minutes, and this audience is defined in the brief as "senior enough to distrust a marketing claim." One disproved claim in the comments discounts the ten true ones around it.
findings.evidence: docs/agents.md:112 "the conductor is your own session" · docs/self-improvement.md:57 "A retro that changes nothing is a correct, common outcome" · docs/hooks.md:302 "this gate is not a guarantee that a secret cannot be published" · docs/evidence-gate.md:15 "This gate blocks SILENCE, not FORGERY"

findings.point: THE ONE LINE IN THE OPERATOR'S BRIEF THE PRODUCT CANNOT RENDER: "you can see how much money did you save with tyran on tokens." Spend shows what the work COST. Money exists at all only under a rate card the operator wrote themselves, the card's name travels with every amount, and nothing anywhere computes a counterfactual. There is no saved-dollars tile, and there should not be one. The replacement is stronger, not weaker: play the real "by model" ranked chart, where the expensive tier is a sliver and the cheap tier carries the volume — that IS the savings argument, made as evidence instead of as a number — and say "It doesn't tell you what you saved. It tells you what you spent. By model, by agent, by ticket. That's the first bill you can actually check."
findings.why: This is the highest-risk claim in the slate and also the easiest upgrade in it. A fabricated savings tile is a feature that does not exist; the top comment says so; and it discredits the tiers argument, which is the whole video. The honest version converts the weakest claim into the most credible one, because "here is the bill" cannot be argued with.
findings.evidence: docs/cost.md:33 "Tokens are facts, money is an opinion" · README.md:88-89 "Money appears only under a rate card you write: Tyran does not know what you pay."

findings.point: THREE ANALOGIES FOR FRESH CONTEXT, RANKED. (1) THE NEW HIRE WHO WASN'T IN THE MEETING — "You brief them on the ticket, not on the last six weeks. And they can't inherit the room's bad assumption, because they weren't in the room." Best: it carries the cost argument and the quality argument in one image, and it is the operator's own frame. (2) SCROLLBACK — "One chat re-reads the whole conversation before every single turn. A subagent opens a clean terminal." The developer-native, bill-shaped one; best where the viewer is a practitioner. (3) THE SLACK THREAD — "You are paying to re-read the entire thread out loud before every sentence you say." The most physically felt; best for short-form, where you get exactly one image. Honest caveat that must bound all three: never quantify it. Cache reads make re-reading far cheaper than the naive arithmetic, and the repo's own measurement says the lever is context size and turn count, not the price of a model.
findings.why: "Fresh context" is the operator's central technical insight and the single hardest thing to draw. All three land in under four seconds of speech, and each one is also a storyboard: a new hire at a desk, a terminal cleared, a thread scrolled.
findings.evidence: Operator: "by creating subagents, the subagent is starting with a fresh context, so it doesn't need to re-read the entire conversation" · README.md:136 "the lever is context size and turn count, not the price of a model"

findings.point: THE COST ARGUMENT IN MANAGER LANGUAGE, RANKED. (1) "You don't put your principal engineer on the grep." — the operator's own thought, a management truth nobody argues with, and a 1:1 map onto the routing table. (2) "A scout reports what a file says. A stronger model doesn't make the file say something else." — near-verbatim from the docs, and the version that survives a skeptic, because it argues about where model strength changes the OUTCOME rather than about a price list. (3) "Tyran doesn't make the model cheaper. It makes the context smaller." — the honest lever, and the sentence that explains why the bill moves at all. (4) "Good teams aren't cheap because they hire cheap people. They're cheap because nobody senior is doing work a junior could do." — the summary closer for the tiers cut. Then stop talking and show the Spend tab.
findings.why: The naive pitch ("cheap models save money") is both weaker and refutable. Ranking these gives every cut a phrasing at the length it can afford, and (2) is the one to reach for whenever a shot has to survive a technical viewer.
findings.evidence: docs/agents.md:118 "A scout reports what a file says; a stronger model does not make the file say something else."

findings.point: THE RECURRING MOTIF: ONE UNBROKEN GOLD THREAD, AND IT IS THE TICKET. The brief already commits to a gold lash-stroke planted early and completing into the jackal lockup — give it a job. The thread is drawn the instant the operator speaks, becomes the hairline edge of a card, runs the lane, lights an agent chip, returns as a question in Waiting on you, and in the landing frame closes into the lash. One line, never cut, never re-drawn. The payoff is the loop closing, which is simultaneously the brand mark and the strongest product claim: nothing you said was dropped. Two supporting motifs: an audio one — a single soft brass tick each time a request becomes a card, counted rather than sprinkled, with the final tick landing on the lockup; and a discipline one — red appears at most twice in any video, always a refusal, so it keeps meaning.
findings.why: A purely graphic motif is decoration and reads as such. Binding the thread to the ticket makes the most abstract claim in the slate ("he never loses a request") visible in every scene without a word of voiceover, and gives the landing frame something to complete rather than a logo to freeze on — which the negative list forbids anyway.
findings.evidence: video/BRIEF.md:69-71 "A single gold lash-stroke, planted early at low weight, completing in the landing frame" · docs/board.md:9 "Moving a ticket IS appending an event."

findings.point: TWELVE CLOSING LINES, RANKED — VERDICT ON THE INCUMBENT: CONFIRMED, BUT DEMOTED TO THE LOCKUP. (1) "The more you use it, the better it gets." — keep it, drawn, in the final frame of every cut; it is already the README h3 and the site hero, and consistency across surfaces is free brand equity. But it promises the future, so it cannot be the only closer on a 28-second cut. Pair it. (2) "You still make every call that matters. You just stop doing the work that doesn't." — best spoken hero closer; it answers the exact fear the manager metaphor creates. (3) "Go to bed. Read the board in the morning." — the most concrete benefit in the slate; board/overnight cut. (4) "Nothing you said is in the scrollback. It's on the board." — the never-forgets cut. (5) "Stop being the manager. Start being the stakeholder." — sharpest positioning; once per slate. (6) "One chat, one model, one person doing everything. Or a team." — closes the loop on the opening mistake; tiers cut. (7) "It doesn't tell you what you saved. It tells you what you spent." — the cost cut. (8) "The gate doesn't ask the agent nicely." — the gates cut; a mechanism line, not a guarantee. (9) "A team that writes down what it learned. In your repo." — the retro cut. (10) "It's not a bigger model. It's a better org chart." — memorable, but the closest the slate ever gets to corporate; at most once, never in the hero. (11) "Open source. Apache two. Two commands." — functional, unemotional; drawn only, on the silent README loop. (12) "Tyran remembers." — REJECT: with this name it reads as surveillance, and it points the memory at the human instead of at the work. Separately, demote "Principal rates for junior work" from closer to OPENER — it is a diagnosis and belongs at 0s.
findings.why: The incumbent is right and also insufficient alone: it is a compounding promise, and short-form needs a present-tense payoff before a future-tense one. Splitting the job — spoken penultimate line per cut, drawn lockup line everywhere — keeps the brand consistent and stops five videos ending identically.
findings.evidence: README.md:21 · site/src/components/landing/Hero.astro:70 "The more you use it, the better it gets."

findings.point: WHERE THIS READS AS CORPORATE, AND THE ANTIDOTES. (a) Scrum vocabulary: a kanban board is on screen, so the temptation is enormous — never narrate sprint, standup, grooming, story points, velocity. The board is a WINDOW, not a ceremony. (b) Corporate nouns: no alignment, resources, headcount, synergy, bandwidth, "levelling up." The metaphor must be carried entirely by WHO DOES WHAT TASK, never by the vocabulary of management. (c) "Stakeholder": electric once, in the operator's own phrasing, and cringe by the third use — budget one per video. (d) "Junior": use the principal/junior frame exactly ONCE per video, as the explanation, then switch permanently to the role names that actually ship — scout, implementer, reviewer. Repeated, it reads as contempt for real juniors, on channels full of them. (e) Anthropomorphism creep: one "he" per video, at the introduction; after that Tyran does things mechanically. Sustained "he" slides into the AI-buddy register this audience distrusts on sight. (f) Demotion anxiety — "if Tyran is the manager, what am I?" — must be answered explicitly inside the first twenty seconds, not implied at the end.
findings.why: Every one of these is a way to lose a senior developer in under two seconds, and four of the six are things a competent copywriter does by reflex. Naming them makes them checkable at script review instead of discoverable at launch.
findings.evidence: Operator: "a principal engineer is not doing scouting or research or basic stupid work that can be done by a junior like in a regular engineering team."

findings.point: THE NAME IS A LIABILITY IN EXACTLY ONE DIRECTION, AND ONE RULE FIXES IT. "Tyran" plus "a manager" plus "never forgets" is one short step from surveillance, and the audience will take that step for free. The rule: TYRAN IS TYRANNICAL TOWARD THE AGENTS AND NEVER TOWARD YOU. Every refusal on screen points at an agent — a report bounced for carrying no output, a commit refused, a write denied by class. Never show Tyran denying, correcting, nagging, timing or measuring the human. The board is a one-way mirror pointed at the team. Corollary for the retro beat: its subject is the TEAM's behaviour, not yours — write "it noticed it kept asking you the same shallow question," never "it noticed you were annoyed." The product itself is built this way: the mistakes ledger has no read channel into your sessions, on purpose.
findings.why: This is the difference between a video that reads as "you finally have a team" and one that reads as "software that watches you." The second reading is available for free to anyone in a bad mood, and it kills the warmth the operator asked for in the same breath as the energy.
findings.evidence: docs/self-improvement.md:125 "nothing — there is no read channel, on purpose" · Operator: "if the questions that you were asking or answering were annoying you, the agents will notice it"

findings.point: "TOO LITTLE BOARD" IS A STRUCTURAL NOTE, NOT A SHOT NOTE — THE BOARD IS THE SECOND CHARACTER. Budget: board on screen within the first twelve seconds of any cut over twenty seconds; at least 40% of hero runtime; at least 60% of the board cut; and the last product image before the lockup is ALWAYS the board, never a terminal. And it must MOVE — three animations that are flashy and also literally true of the product: (a) the open-question count incrementing inside the "Waiting on you" tab label while the viewer is looking at a different tab; (b) a card crossing a lane at the instant an event is appended, because moving a ticket IS appending an event; (c) an agent chip aging through its four colours, and a card in a stalled lane showing how long it has stood still. The four Overview tiles — waiting on you · agents running · progress · needs a human — are a ready-made HUD and should be the frame the hero returns to between beats, the way a film returns to an establishing shot.
findings.why: The operator's complaint cannot be satisfied by adding board shots to the end; it needs the board to be where the story happens. These three animations also solve the harder problem — a still screenshot of a kanban board is inert, and panning across it reads as a slideshow.
findings.evidence: docs/board.md:200 "The queue's tab label carries its open count" · docs/board.md:392 "Cards say how long they have stood still." · Operator: "the board is the flashy thing users will want"

findings.point: FIVE PROOF BEATS ALREADY IN THE REPO THAT ARE BETTER THAN ANYTHING A COPYWRITER WILL INVENT, AND ALL TRUE. (1) "Answering *what is going on* meant opening 31 files." — the cold open for the board cut. (2) "A scout reports what a file says. A stronger model doesn't make the file say something else." — the tiers cut's entire argument in one sentence. (3) The loudest agent used to have the freshest chip on the board, so the board now sorts on what an agent SHOWED rather than what it SAID — the most manager-flavoured detail in the whole product and completely unused so far. (4) and (5) The two real questions from the sandbox, verbatim, for any shot of Waiting on you: "The board reloads itself every 30 seconds, which wipes a half-typed model name. Pause the refresh while the Settings tab is open, or keep the page always-live and accept the loss?" and "Should the board be able to WRITE at all? Once it can, 'read-only board on loopback' stops being true, and that sentence is currently load-bearing in the docs."
findings.why: The operator's retro pitch turns on agents not asking shallow questions — and these two questions ARE the proof, because a viewer reads them and thinks "a person wrote that." Invented placeholder questions do the opposite. All five happened; the sandbox is the initiatives that built the board itself.
findings.evidence: docs/board.md:7 · docs/agents.md:118 · docs/board.md:427-437 "Signal is not evidence" · site/sandbox/settings-editor.jsonl

findings.point: THE VOICE NOTE THE METAPHOR ALREADY ANSWERS: READ IT AS THE MANAGER, NOT ABOUT THE MANAGER. A handover, not a pitch — confident, warm, unhurried, verb early, last word landed, and no line that needs a breath in the middle. Sentence architecture does more here than the TTS direction string: short declaratives hold 85-92% speech density without the read sounding chased, while stacked subordinate clauses force the reader either to rush or to breathe, which is precisely what produced both complaints in sequence. Two mechanical consequences for the script files: a mid-sentence em-dash renders as a pause, so convert them to full stops in the spoken text and keep the dash only in the caption; and no spoken sentence should exceed roughly fourteen words.
findings.why: It gives the VO director a single instruction that both notes can be checked against, instead of a dial between "more excited" and "less excited" that will keep overshooting. It is also the cheapest fix available — most of it happens in the script, before a single sample is synthesized.
findings.evidence: video/scripts/vo.json:27 "A scout does the reconnaissance — cheap, fast, read-only." · Operator: "The pauses are too long between sentences."

recommendations: Adopt the three-length through-line as the slate's claim boundary: every cut is a subset of the paragraph, and no video introduces a claim that is not in it. Put the paragraph at the top of vo.json as a comment so writers cannot drift from it.

Rewrite the cost beat everywhere: delete every implication of measured savings, and land "It doesn't tell you what you saved. It tells you what you spent — by model, by agent, by ticket. That's the first bill you can actually check" over the real by-model chart with the top tier as a visible sliver.

Fix the contradiction between the fresh-context beat and the memory beat with one formulation used slate-wide: "Each agent starts clean. The team remembers." The journal is the memory; the agent is not.

Move the board earlier and keep it longer in every cut, to the budget in the board finding, and animate the three honest motions — the tab-label count incrementing, a card crossing a lane on the event, a chip aging — rather than panning across a still capture.

Answer "if he's the manager, what am I?" out loud before 0:20 in the hero: you are the stakeholder, you keep every decision, and the proof is a tab called Waiting on you with a live count in its label.

Give the gold thread the ticket's job — drawn when you speak, becoming the card edge, the lane, the chip, the question, and finally closing into the lash — and never cut it. The landing frame is a loop closing, not a logo appearing.
Use the principal/junior frame exactly once per video, as the explanation, then switch permanently to scout / implementer / reviewer. Budget one "he" and one "stakeholder" per video.

Put the two real sandbox questions on screen verbatim in every cut that shows Waiting on you — the 30-second refresh wiping a half-typed model name, and whether the board should be able to write at all.

Assign closers per cut from the ranked twelve, keep "The more you use it, the better it gets" as the drawn lockup in all of them, and give each cut its own spoken penultimate line so five videos do not end identically.

Rewrite the retro beat from mood-reading to behaviour-counting: "Overrule it in the same place three times and it becomes a rule. Five times and it becomes law." Put the 3 → knowledge, 5 → law graphic on screen while it is said, and never promise that a retro changes something every time.
Convert every mid-sentence em-dash in the spoken text to a full stop and cap spoken sentences at about fourteen words; keep the dashes in captions only, where the realignment restores them.

Add a claim-check pass before render: every spoken sentence must trace to a mechanism in docs/ at the specificity the docs use. Mechanism verbs only — refuses, appends, routes, records, holds back — never guarantee verbs: prevents, ensures, can't, impossible.
doNot: Do not say or render "you saved $X" / "saved N% of tokens" — no such number exists in the product; money only appears under a rate card the operator wrote.
Do not claim secrets "can't leak" or that the gate makes leaking impossible. The true and defensible claim is "a commit carrying a secret is refused."
Do not claim the evidence gate makes reports honest. It refuses a report that shows you nothing; it does not detect a fabricated number.
Do not animate agent-to-agent chat bubbles. State moves through one committed journal and knowledge briefs — which is the stronger claim, because it survives a restart.
Do not call subagents stateful or say each agent "remembers." The team remembers; each agent starts clean, and that is the whole fresh-context argument.
Do not quantify the token saving with a multiple or a percentage. Cache reads make the naive arithmetic wrong, and the lever is context size and turn count.
Do not show Tyran as a character or process standing beside the operator making a decision — the conductor is the operator's own session.
Do not show Tyran refusing, correcting, nagging, timing or measuring the HUMAN. Every refusal on screen points at an agent.
Do not use scrum vocabulary — sprint, standup, backlog grooming, story points, velocity — over a kanban board. The board is a window, not a ceremony.
Do not use corporate nouns: alignment, resources, headcount, synergy, bandwidth, levelling up.
Do not repeat "junior" or "stakeholder" past one use per video, and do not sustain "he" past the introduction.
Do not close on "Tyran remembers" or any line that points the memory at the operator rather than at the work.
Do not scale the 2240px board capture into a 9:16 frame — rebuild the board natively in the board tokens; and never put browser chrome around it.
Do not end on a frozen logo, a light theme, a purple-blue gradient, bokeh, a stock developer, or a still board. The last product image is a board still ticking.
Do not write a slash command to be spoken literally — phonetic in the VO, real command drawn on screen.

scores.angle: You didn't install a tool, you hired a manager — and every mechanism in Tyran (routing, the board, the gates, the retro) is shown as something a good manager does, with the token saving arriving late, as the consequence of delegating well rather than the reason to watch.
scores.weakness: It opens on a claim with zero evidence behind it. 'You didn't install a tool. You hired someone.' is the exact sentence every AI launch video I have already closed opens with, and shot 01 is an empty card — I am being asked to accept the most anthropomorphic framing in the slate before I have seen a single mechanism. Worse, the operator's own strongest argument (one chat, one model, every job, and that is why your bill is high) is never SPOKEN anywhere in the cut; it exists only as a wordless split-screen at line 07. The rationale defends the money beat arriving seventeenth as an artistic choice, but for this audience it means eighty seconds pass before the film tells me what problem I have. Deepest pillar coverage in the slate, wrapped in the least credible first ten seconds.

scores.angle: Open on the viewer's own last session — the expensive model renaming a variable — name the mistake in twelve seconds, then spend the remaining two minutes paying it off on the board, where every claim has a receipt.
scores.weakness: Line 19 is overloaded and contains the only genuinely cheap shot in the slate: the ghosted counterfactual frame carrying 'a key published is a key burned' rising and being pushed back down. explainer.purpose: The flagship 16:9 explainer: open on the viewer's own last session (the expensive model renaming a variable), turn on the manager who deploys a routed team, then pay every claim off on the live board — where the aside you mutter mid-run becomes ticket T-9 — and close on the retro that writes what it learned into your repo.
